header: 4Audit: are there test samples in the training sets?

images.caption: Figure 3:Three kinds of duplicates, each with a real example. (a) Exact duplicate: the same image file and candidate appear in the Polaris test set and in the Spica training set with the same eight ratings (one square per rating, darker is higher), and in the Nebula training set with the same mean. (b) Re-encoded image: one photograph stored as two files of equal size in pixels whose hashes differ; it is found only by feature similarity. (c) Near-identical caption: the same image, a candidate that differs by an article and a period.

header: 7A protocol without duplicates, and a re-ranking

images.caption: Figure 11:Two pairs from the Polaris test set. Each row shows the image, the candidate (in quotation marks), one of the references, and the mean human score on a 0–1 scale. On the right, a bar gives the percentile at which a metric places the pair among all pairs of the set that are rated above the lowest score, and the dashed line gives the percentile of the human score. (a) The candidate names two women where the image shows a woman and a man; learned and embedding metrics rate it high, the judge rates it low, as people do. (b) A duplicated sample: Pearl trained without it underrates the pair, and Pearl trained with it (orange) moves most of the way to the human score. Twelve further cases:J.
